title: Flutter & Dart Fundamentals
summary: The widget tree, the build method's contract, and the real state-management landscape in Flutter — from setState to Provider, Riverpod, and Bloc.

slides.markdown:
Flutter's core idea, inherited conceptually from the same declarative-UI lineage as SwiftUI and React: **everything is a widget**, and a widget describes what the UI should look like for the current configuration rather than mutating anything imperatively. What's distinct to Flutter is the three-tree architecture underneath — widget, element, render — that makes that description cheap to rebuild constantly.

This topic covers that architecture, the Stateless/Stateful split, and honestly surveys the state-management landscape beyond `setState`, since 'which state management library' is one of the first real decisions any Flutter team makes.

slides.subTitle: composing UI from small pieces
slides.markdown:
In Flutter, padding is a widget (`Padding`), centering is a widget (`Center`), even a widget that does nothing but constrain its child's size is a widget (`SizedBox`). There's no separate 'layout system' bolted onto a widget tree — layout **is** composition: you wrap widgets in other widgets to get the effect you want.

```dart
Center(
  child: Padding(
    padding: EdgeInsets.all(16),
    child: Text('Hello, Flutter'),
  ),
)
```

This composability is deliberate and pervasive: instead of a `TextView` with a dozen properties for alignment, padding, and background, Flutter gives you small, single-purpose widgets you nest. It reads more verbosely at first, but each piece is independently understandable and reusable — you can extract any subtree into its own named widget without special ceremony.

slides.sectionTitle: The widget, element, and render trees
slides.markdown: ![Flutter's widget, element, and render trees and how configuration flows between them](assets/flutter-three-trees.svg)

assets.alt: Flutter's widget, element, and render trees and how configuration flows between them

slides.markdown:
| | StatelessWidget | StatefulWidget |
|---|---|---|
| Holds mutable data? | no — immutable configuration only | yes, via an associated State object |
| Rebuilds when | its parent rebuilds with new configuration | its own State calls setState, or parent rebuilds |
| Lifecycle hooks | just build() | initState, dispose, and others, on the State object |
| Typical use | pure presentation from passed-in data | anything with local, changing data (a counter, a form field, an animation) |

The split exists because a widget itself is thrown away and recreated on every rebuild — it cannot hold onto data across rebuilds. `StatefulWidget` solves this by creating a separate, longer-lived `State` object that persists across rebuilds even as the widget configuration around it is recreated, mirroring exactly the problem `@State` solves in SwiftUI.

slides.subTitle: fast and pure
slides.markdown:
`build()` can be called by the framework far more often than intuition suggests — any time an ancestor rebuilds, any time `setState` is called on this widget or a parent, any time an inherited value it depends on changes. Two rules follow directly:

- **It must be fast.** Expensive work (a network call, heavy computation) inside `build()` reruns on every single rebuild, not just when the underlying data actually changed.
- **It must be pure** — no side effects (starting a timer, making a network call, mutating external state) should live inside `build()`, because you can't control or predict how many times or when it runs. Side effects belong in lifecycle methods like `initState()` or in response to explicit user actions.

A `build()` method that fetches data directly is a very common beginner bug: it refetches on every rebuild, including rebuilds triggered by completely unrelated state changes elsewhere in the tree.

slides.sectionTitle: State management options at a glance
slides.subTitle: setState, Provider, Riverpod, Bloc
slides.markdown:
| | setState | Provider | Riverpod | Bloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | one widget's local state | app-wide, via widget tree (InheritedWidget-based) | app-wide, compile-time safe, not tied to widget tree | app-wide, explicit event-to-state stream pattern |
| Boilerplate | minimal | low | low-medium | higher, but very structured |
| Testability | poor for shared state | good | very good (no BuildContext needed) | very good (pure functions, easy to unit test) |
| Best fit | one screen's local UI state | small-to-medium apps, straightforward shared state | teams wanting compile-time safety and easy testing | larger teams wanting a strict, auditable event/state contract |

There's no single 'correct' choice — the honest answer in an interview is to name the trade-off (simplicity vs testability vs strictness) rather than declaring one universally best, since production Flutter apps genuinely use all four depending on team size and how disciplined the codebase needs to be.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: setState on a disposed widget
Pitfall: rebuilding an expensive subtree from state too high
slides.markdown:
Calling `setState` on a widget high in the tree — say, a screen's root `StatefulWidget` — rebuilds **everything beneath it** by default, including large, expensive subtrees (a complex chart, a long static list) that have nothing to do with the specific piece of state that changed.

The fix is pushing state ownership down to the smallest widget that actually needs it, so `setState` only rebuilds the narrow subtree affected — extracting the piece that changes into its own small `StatefulWidget`, or using `const` constructors on subtrees that never change (Flutter skips rebuilding widgets it can prove are unchanged via `const`). This is the same 'don't rebuild the whole tree' discipline every declarative UI framework needs, just with Flutter's specific tools (`const`, extracting widgets, `Consumer`/`Selector` in Provider/Riverpod for scoping rebuilds to exactly the data read) for enforcing it.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior nuance: widget identity via keys
slides.markdown:
Flutter's element tree matches new widget configurations to existing elements primarily by **type and position** in the tree — the same identity-by-structure idea as SwiftUI. Reordering a list of stateful widgets without giving each a stable `Key` makes Flutter match by position rather than by logical identity, so item 3's `State` can end up attached to what's now item 1's widget after a reorder — a subtle bug where per-item state (an expanded/collapsed flag, a text field's cursor position) appears to jump to the wrong item.

The fix is a `ValueKey` or `ObjectKey` derived from stable data (an item's unique ID), not its list index — exactly the same discipline as SwiftUI's `ForEach` wanting a stable identifier, because both frameworks solve the identity problem the same way: infer from structure unless told otherwise via an explicit key.
